title: 08 — Delta Lake
html:
08 — Delta Lake

The one idea: a Delta table is a folder of ordinary Parquet files plus an ordered log that says which of those files form the table at each version. Every feature — ACID, time travel, MERGE, schema enforcement, change feeds — is a consequence of writing that log carefully and reading it first.

1. What is on disk

sales/
├── _delta_log/
│   ├── 00000000000000000000.json      ← version 0 (CREATE / first write)
│   ├── 00000000000000000001.json      ← version 1
│   ├── ...
│   ├── 00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet   ← snapshot of state at version 10
│   ├── 00000000000000000011.json
│   └── _last_checkpoint               ← pointer to the latest checkpoint
├── part-00000-3f1c...-c000.snappy.parquet
├── part-00001-9a7e...-c000.snappy.parquet
└── deletion_vector_...bin             ← only if deletion vectors are in use

Each JSON commit file contains actions:

Action Meaning
add A data file now belongs to the table (with path, size, partition values and column statistics: min, max, null count, row count)
remove A data file no longer belongs to the table (it stays on disk until VACUUM)
metaData Schema, partition columns, table properties
protocol Minimum reader/writer versions or table features a client must support
commitInfo Who/what/when: operation, parameters, metrics
txn Application transaction IDs, used for idempotent writes from streaming or foreachBatch

To read the table at version N, a reader loads the latest checkpoint at or before N, replays the JSON commits after it, and ends up with the exact set of live files and the current schema. It then prunes that file list using the statistics before opening any Parquet file.

Checkpoints are written periodically (every 10 commits by default in classic Delta; newer versions can use other policies) so readers never have to replay thousands of small JSON files.

2. ACID on object storage

Object stores have no multi-file transactions. Delta gets atomicity from one rule: a commit happens at the instant file N.json is created, and only one writer can create it. The storage layer must offer "put if absent" (or Delta uses a coordination mechanism where the store lacks it).

Property How Delta provides it
Atomicity Data files are written first (invisible, since no log entry references them). The commit file is written last, atomically. A crash before the commit leaves only orphan files, which VACUUM later removes.
Consistency Schema enforcement and constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK) are validated before commit.
Isolation Readers use a snapshot (one version) for the whole query; writers use optimistic concurrency control.
Durability Committed files live in durable cloud storage.

Optimistic concurrency control

---
title: Optimistic concurrency — two writers race for the same version
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Writer A
    participant L as _delta_log
    participant B as Writer B
    A->>L: Read latest version (10)
    B->>L: Read latest version (10)
    A->>A: Write new data files
    B->>B: Write new data files
    A->>L: Create 11.json (succeeds)
    B->>L: Create 11.json (fails, already exists)
    B->>L: Read what version 11 changed
    B->>B: Check for logical conflict
    B->>L: No conflict, so create 12.json

If the other commit touched data this writer read or changed (for example both updated files in the same partition), the retry fails with a conflict exception such as ConcurrentAppendException or ConcurrentDeleteReadException. Common ways to reduce conflicts:

  • Make concurrent jobs touch disjoint data and put that in the predicate (MERGE ... ON t.id = s.id AND t.date = '2026-09-24'), so conflict detection can see they do not overlap.
  • Use row-level concurrency (available on Databricks with deletion vectors and liquid clustering), which detects conflicts at row rather than file level.
  • Serialise writers to one table through the orchestrator where possible.

Isolation levels: WriteSerializable (default; writes are serialisable, reads may see a snapshot that is not strictly serial with writes) and Serializable (stricter, more conflicts).

3. Time travel

DESCRIBE HISTORY silver.orders;                       -- versions, operations, who, metrics

SELECT * FROM silver.orders VERSION AS OF 42;
SELECT * FROM silver.orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-09-24T06:00:00';

-- What changed between two versions? (simple diff)
SELECT * FROM silver.orders VERSION AS OF 43
EXCEPT
SELECT * FROM silver.orders VERSION AS OF 42;

-- Undo a bad write
RESTORE TABLE silver.orders TO VERSION AS OF 42;

df = spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 42).table("silver.orders")

Time travel is limited by two retention settings:

  • delta.logRetentionDuration (default 30 days): how long commit history is kept.
  • delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration (default 7 days): the minimum age before VACUUM may delete removed data files.

You can only travel to a version whose data files still exist. Time travel is a safety net for days or weeks, not a substitute for backups or for SCD history.

4. MERGE INTO

MERGE matches source rows to target rows on a condition and applies clauses:

MERGE INTO target t
USING source s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_deleted THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (id, name, updated_at) VALUES (s.id, s.name, s.updated_at)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;   -- target rows absent from source (full-snapshot sync)

Rules that save you pain:

  1. The source must have at most one row per match key. If two source rows match the same target row, MERGE fails ("multiple source rows matched"). Deduplicate first.
  2. Put partition or clustering filters in the ON clause when you know the affected range, so fewer files are scanned and rewritten.
  3. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE compares against the entire target unless you add a condition — only use it when the source is a complete snapshot.
  4. Clauses are evaluated in order; the first matching clause wins.

Full SCD type 2 example

Target dimension:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS gold.dim_customer (
  customer_sk  BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  customer_id  STRING NOT NULL,
  name         STRING,
  city         STRING,
  valid_from   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  valid_to     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  is_current   BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);

Incoming batch silver.customer_updates(customer_id, name, city, updated_at) may contain several changes per customer; keep the latest.

The trick: one MERGE must both close the old version (an update) and insert the new version for the same customer. A single source row can only do one of those, so we feed each changed customer in twice: once with a real merge_key (matches the current row → close it) and once with a NULL merge_key (never matches → insert the new version).

---
title: SCD2 merge — each changed key enters the MERGE twice
---
flowchart LR
    U["Latest update per customer"] --> A["Copy 1<br/>merge_key = customer_id"]
    U --> C{"Attributes changed<br/>vs current row?"}
    C -->|"yes"| B["Copy 2<br/>merge_key = NULL"]
    A --> M["MERGE on merge_key<br/>and is_current"]
    B --> M
    M -->|"matched and changed"| X["Close old row<br/>valid_to, is_current = false"]
    M -->|"not matched"| Y["Insert new current row<br/>(new or changed customer)"]

SQL

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW customer_changes AS
SELECT customer_id, name, city, updated_at
FROM (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM silver.customer_updates
) WHERE rn = 1;

MERGE INTO gold.dim_customer AS t
USING (
  -- Copy 1: every incoming customer, keyed normally
  SELECT c.customer_id AS merge_key, c.*
  FROM customer_changes c

  UNION ALL

  -- Copy 2: only customers whose tracked attributes changed, with a NULL key
  SELECT NULL AS merge_key, c.*
  FROM customer_changes c
  JOIN gold.dim_customer d
    ON c.customer_id = d.customer_id AND d.is_current
  WHERE NOT (c.name <=> d.name) OR NOT (c.city <=> d.city)
) AS u
ON t.customer_id = u.merge_key AND t.is_current

WHEN MATCHED AND (NOT (t.name <=> u.name) OR NOT (t.city <=> u.city)) THEN
  UPDATE SET t.is_current = false,
             t.valid_to   = u.updated_at

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (customer_id, name, city, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
  VALUES (u.customer_id, u.name, u.city, u.updated_at, TIMESTAMP'9999-12-31 00:00:00', true);

How each case plays out:

Case Copy 1 (merge_key = id) Copy 2 (merge_key = NULL) Result
Brand-new customer Not matched → insert Not produced (no current row to join) One new current row
Existing, attributes changed Matched and changed → close old row Not matched → insert Old row closed, new current row
Existing, nothing changed Matched but condition false → no-op Not produced No change

<=> is the null-safe equality operator, so a change from NULL to a value is detected. Rerunning the same batch is a no-op after the first run, so the job is idempotent.

PySpark

from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

tracked = ["name", "city"]
changed_cond = " OR ".join(f"NOT (t.{c} <=> u.{c})" for c in tracked)

w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at").desc())
latest = (spark.table("silver.customer_updates")
          .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
          .filter("rn = 1")
          .drop("rn"))

dim = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "gold.dim_customer")
current = dim.toDF().filter("is_current")

changed = (latest.alias("u")
           .join(current.alias("t"), F.col("u.customer_id") == F.col("t.customer_id"))
           .where(changed_cond)
           .select("u.*"))

staged = (latest.withColumn("merge_key", F.col("customer_id"))
          .unionByName(changed.withColumn("merge_key", F.lit(None).cast("string"))))

(dim.alias("t")
    .merge(staged.alias("u"), "t.customer_id = u.merge_key AND t.is_current = true")
    .whenMatchedUpdate(
        condition=changed_cond,
        set={"is_current": F.lit(False), "valid_to": F.col("u.updated_at")})
    .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={
        "customer_id": F.col("u.customer_id"),
        "name":        F.col("u.name"),
        "city":        F.col("u.city"),
        "valid_from":  F.col("u.updated_at"),
        "valid_to":    F.lit("9999-12-31 00:00:00").cast("timestamp"),
        "is_current":  F.lit(True)})
    .execute())

Edge cases to decide explicitly:

  • Late updates: an update whose updated_at is older than the current row's valid_from should not become current. Filter them out or route them to a correction process.
  • Deletes: typically close the current row (is_current = false, valid_to = delete time) and optionally mark is_deleted, rather than physically deleting history.
  • Multiple changes per batch: the example keeps only the latest; if you need every intermediate version, process changes in order per key or use the declarative pipelines' APPLY CHANGES / AUTO CDC with SCD type 2, which handles sequencing for you.

5. Schema enforcement vs schema evolution

Enforcement (default): a write whose schema is incompatible with the table fails. Extra columns, missing NOT NULL columns or incompatible types are rejected. This is what stops a producer's accidental change from polluting silver.

Evolution (opt-in): allow compatible changes to be applied to the table schema.

# Append with new columns added to the table schema
(df.write.format("delta")
   .mode("append")
   .option("mergeSchema", "true")
   .saveAsTable("bronze.events"))

# Replace schema entirely (e.g. type change) when overwriting
(df.write.format("delta")
   .mode("overwrite")
   .option("overwriteSchema", "true")
   .saveAsTable("silver.events"))

-- Evolve the schema as part of a MERGE (recent Databricks runtimes)
MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION INTO silver.customers t
USING updates s ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

-- Explicit DDL
ALTER TABLE silver.customers ADD COLUMNS (loyalty_tier STRING);
Change How
Add a column mergeSchema, schema evolution in MERGE, or ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS
Rename or drop a column Enable column mapping (delta.columnMapping.mode = 'name'), then ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN / DROP COLUMN without rewriting data
Widen a type (int → bigint) Type widening feature on recent runtimes, otherwise rewrite with overwriteSchema
Narrow or incompatible type change Rewrite the table

A sensible policy: allow evolution in bronze (never lose incoming data), enforce strictly in silver and gold (changes go through code review).

6. OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER and liquid clustering

-- Compact small files (bin-packing)
OPTIMIZE silver.orders;

-- Compact and co-locate by columns (non-clustered tables)
OPTIMIZE silver.orders ZORDER BY (customer_id);

-- Liquid clustering: define keys once, OPTIMIZE clusters incrementally
ALTER TABLE silver.orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id, order_date);
OPTIMIZE silver.orders;

-- Force re-clustering of all data (after changing keys, for example)
OPTIMIZE silver.orders FULL;
  • OPTIMIZE is idempotent and transactional; readers are unaffected, and old files become remove actions.
  • Z-order and liquid clustering are mutually exclusive on a table; liquid clustering is the recommended path for new tables.
  • Clustering on the merge key makes MERGE touch fewer files.
  • On Unity Catalog managed tables, predictive optimization can schedule OPTIMIZE (and VACUUM) automatically.

Layout background is in Storage Formats and Layout.

7. VACUUM and retention

VACUUM permanently deletes data files that are no longer referenced by any table version within the retention window, plus orphan files from failed writes.

VACUUM silver.orders;                  -- default retention: 7 days
VACUUM silver.orders RETAIN 168 HOURS; -- explicit
VACUUM silver.orders DRY RUN;          -- list what would be deleted
  • Until VACUUM runs, deleted and overwritten data still exists in storage. This matters for cost (storage grows with every rewrite) and for GDPR (a "deleted" customer is still recoverable via time travel).
  • Retention below 7 days is blocked by a safety check unless you disable it. Do not: a long-running reader or a streaming query that is behind may still need those files.
  • VACUUM does not delete the _delta_log; log entries expire according to delta.logRetentionDuration when checkpoints are written.
  • With deletion vectors, a soft-deleted row remains in its Parquet file until the file is rewritten; run REORG TABLE t APPLY (PURGE) then VACUUM when you must physically remove data.

8. Change Data Feed

Change Data Feed (CDF) records row-level changes so consumers can process only what changed, including updates and deletes.

ALTER TABLE silver.customers SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true);

-- Changes between versions 5 and 10
SELECT * FROM table_changes('silver.customers', 5, 10);

Extra columns in the feed:

Column Values
_change_type insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete
_commit_version Table version of the change
_commit_timestamp Commit time 
changes = (spark.readStream
           .option("readChangeFeed", "true")
           .table("silver.customers")
           .filter("_change_type != 'update_preimage'"))

Use CDF to propagate silver changes to gold incrementally, to sync to external systems, or to audit. It only records changes made after it is enabled, and the change data is subject to the same retention as the table's files.

9. Deletion vectors

Without deletion vectors, deleting one row from a 1 GB Parquet file means rewriting the whole file (copy-on-write). With deletion vectors, Delta writes a small bitmap marking the row as deleted; readers skip marked rows. Updates become "mark old row deleted + write the new row to a new file".

Copy-on-write Deletion vectors
DELETE / UPDATE / MERGE cost Rewrite every touched file Write small bitmaps plus new rows
Read cost None extra Slight, until files are compacted
Physical removal Immediate on rewrite (after VACUUM) After OPTIMIZE/REORG ... APPLY (PURGE) plus VACUUM

Enable with delta.enableDeletionVectors = true (enabled by default for new tables on recent Databricks runtimes). Readers must support the feature, which matters if external engines read the table.

10. Table properties worth knowing

Property Purpose
delta.enableChangeDataFeed Record row-level changes
delta.enableDeletionVectors Cheaper deletes/updates/merges
delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite Shuffle before write to produce fewer, larger files
delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact Compact small files after writes
delta.targetFileSize Target size for files written by OPTIMIZE and writes
delta.logRetentionDuration How long history is kept (default 30 days)
delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration Minimum age before VACUUM deletes files (default 7 days)
delta.appendOnly Reject updates and deletes (useful for bronze/audit tables)
delta.columnMapping.mode name enables column rename/drop without rewriting
delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols Number of leading columns with statistics collected (default 32)
delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns Explicit list of columns to collect statistics on 
CREATE TABLE bronze.events (
  event_id STRING, payload STRING, _ingested_at TIMESTAMP
)
CLUSTER BY (_ingested_at)
TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.appendOnly' = 'true',
  'delta.enableChangeDataFeed' = 'false',
  'delta.logRetentionDuration' = 'interval 60 days'
);

DESCRIBE DETAIL bronze.events;      -- location, size, file count, properties
SHOW TBLPROPERTIES bronze.events;

Protocol upgrades: enabling some features (deletion vectors, column mapping, liquid clustering) upgrades the table protocol, and older readers or other engines may no longer read the table. Check your consumers before enabling features on shared tables.

Azure / .NET mapping

Need Approach
Storage Delta tables on ADLS Gen2, ideally Unity Catalog managed tables
Reading Delta outside Databricks Microsoft Fabric (Delta is its native table format), Synapse serverless SQL, Power BI via Databricks SQL, the open-source delta-rs library via Python
.NET access Query through a Databricks SQL warehouse (ODBC/JDBC or Statement Execution API) rather than reading Delta files directly
Backup / DR Deep clone to another region's storage on a schedule; storage-account replication alone does not guarantee a consistent log and data snapshot

Review checklist

  • I can describe what is in _delta_log and how a reader reconstructs a version.
  • I can explain how Delta achieves atomic commits on object storage.
  • I can explain optimistic concurrency and how to reduce write conflicts.
  • I can use time travel and know what limits it.
  • I can write an SCD2 MERGE and explain why changed rows appear twice in the source.
  • I know the rule that each target row may match at most one source row.
  • I can distinguish schema enforcement from evolution and set a policy per layer.
  • I know what VACUUM deletes, what it does not, and why short retention is dangerous.
  • I can enable and consume Change Data Feed.
  • I know how deletion vectors change the cost of DELETE/UPDATE/MERGE.
